segments.title: The Fog and What It Hides

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked — a close reading of one of the great novels in the English language.
Over the course of this series, we'll be working through Charles Dickens's vast, ferocious, and extraordinarily beautiful novel — chapter by chapter, layer by layer.
We begin today where Dickens begins: in fog.
Not merely the weather — though the weather is extraordinary — but fog as a condition of mind, of law, of society itself.
Joining me today are three remarkable readers of this novel, each bringing something irreplaceable to the table.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don whose life's work has been the moral imagination of the great Victorian novelists.
Edmund reads Dickens not as a social reformer but as a novelist of character — of goodness tested, weakness revealed, and the soul under pressure.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal and social historian who knows the institutions of Victorian England from the inside out.
When Dickens puts a lawyer in a room or a pauper on a street, James can tell you exactly what that meant — legally, economically, and humanly.
And Dr. Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads novels as anatomies of power.
For Daniel, every fog in Dickens hides a mechanism — and he is very good at finding it.
Let's open the novel — right at the beginning — and see what Dickens does.
The opening of Bleak House is, I think, among the most audacious in all of English prose fiction.
Dickens does not begin with a character, not with a scene in the conventional sense, not even with a complete sentence.
He begins with a word: London.
Just that — a noun dropped into silence, like a stone into a very deep well.
And then this extraordinary sentence arrives — and I want to read it, because it deserves to be heard properly.

"As much mud in the streets as if the waters had but newly retired from the face of the earth, and it would not be wonderful to meet a Megalosaurus, forty feet long or so, waddling like an elephantine lizard up Holborn Hill."
A Megalosaurus — waddling up Holborn Hill.
Dickens has, in a single image, driven London back to the primordial — and the joke is perfect because it is also completely serious.
This is not mere atmosphere-painting. This is a theological statement about what civilisation has become.
Edmund is right that there's a theological dimension — but I'd want to hold that alongside something very specific and material.
Michaelmas term, as Dickens signals immediately — this is the legal term when Chancery is in session.
The fog and the law arrive together from the novel's very first breath.
The Court of Chancery in the 1850s was a genuine catastrophe — cases that ran for decades, estates entirely consumed by legal costs.
Dickens isn't exaggerating Jarndyce and Jarndyce for comic effect. He is, if anything, understating it.

Notice what Dickens does with the mud — foot passengers "adding new deposits to the crust upon crust of mud, sticking at those points tenaciously to the pavement, and accumulating at compound interest."
Compound interest — in a description of mud. That's an economic metaphor buried in filth, and it is entirely deliberate.
The city is literally accruing corruption, layer upon layer, and no one can pay off the debt.
James has put his finger on something I think is central — the fog is not decorative, it is structural.
Dickens shows us a city where every class is degraded by this atmosphere — dogs, horses, foot passengers — and yet the degradation is not equally distributed.
The fog obscures — and what it obscures, systematically, is the relationship between cause and effect.
Consider what Dickens gives us later — a man called Nemo, lying in a filthy room.
"Through the general sickliness and faintness, and the odour of stale tobacco, there comes into the lawyer's mouth the bitter, vapid taste of opium."
The fog has a taste by the time it reaches that room. It is the taste of a life utterly expended and utterly discarded.
And the only witness is Tulkinghorn — the lawyer — who tastes it in his own mouth and feels, we are told, nothing in particular.
That is the system working exactly as designed.
I'll grant Daniel his point about Tulkinghorn — the man is a remarkable creation precisely because his coldness is absolute, and Dickens renders it without flinching.
But I'd resist the idea that atmosphere in Dickens is merely — merely — a political instrument.
There's something here that goes deeper than class critique — something almost eschatological.
The soot, Dickens tells us, is "gone into mourning, one might imagine, for the death of the sun."
The death of the sun. Not the failure of an institution — the extinction of light itself.
Dickens is writing in a tradition that includes Dante and Milton, not only Edwin Chadwick's sanitary reports.
I don't think those things are mutually exclusive — the eschatological and the institutional can occupy the same image.
And the image that haunts me most in this opening movement of the novel is not the fog over London — it's the ghost on the terrace at Chesney Wold.
Dickens gives us the legend of the crippled lady — and her curse, delivered to her husband in the moment of her collapse, is extraordinary.
"I will die here where I have walked. And I will walk here, though I am in my grave.
I will walk here until the pride of this house is humbled. And when calamity or when disgrace is coming to it, let the Dedlocks listen for my step!"
That is a curse perfectly calibrated to the Dedlock story — pride humbled, disgrace incoming.
The ghost doesn't haunt because of the supernatural — she haunts because the institution of aristocratic pride creates its own nemesis.
The fog reaches Chesney Wold too. It just arrives dressed as a ghost.
James's reading of that curse is exactly right — and I'd add one thing.
The crippled lady walked that terrace in pain, every day, without complaint — and no one in the house spoke of it.
Dickens tells us she "never spoke to any one of being crippled or of being in pain" — the house simply accommodated her suffering and moved on.
That is the Dedlock house in miniature — and, I'd argue, the English class system in miniature.
Suffering is absorbed, unseen, until it erupts — as a curse, as a scandal, as a death.
The fog hides it. That's the novel's first, and deepest, argument.
The fog hides it — and in the next segment, we'll follow the fog indoors: into the Court of Chancery itself, and into what Dickens makes of the law.
Edmund, James, Daniel — thank you. We'll be back shortly.

segments.title: The Machinery of Injustice: Jo's Witness

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, the podcast that takes Dickens's great novel apart — passage by passage, institution by institution — to ask what it still has to say.
I'm joined today by three guests who bring very different lenses to this book, and I want to introduce them properly.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don whose life's work has been reading novels as moral drama — stories about character tested by circumstance, about goodness and its costs.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal and social historian who knows exactly what Chancery was, what it did to people, and what it meant to be poor in Victorian England.
And Dr. Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads novels as anatomies of class power — every institution a mechanism, every character a position in a system.
Today we are in Chapter Eleven — the inquest over Nemo, the dead law-writer — and at its centre is Jo, the crossing-sweeper.
Jo is one of the great figures in English fiction, and Dickens introduces him through a piece of courtroom theatre that is also a moral indictment.
Edmund, let's begin with you — with what Jo actually says, and what that testimony reveals.
What strikes me first is not the pathos — though the pathos is overwhelming — but the precision of the prose.
Dickens gives us Jo's testimony in reported speech, and the effect is extraordinary — both clinical and devastating.
Consider what we're told, in that flat, accumulative way:
"No father, no mother, no friends. Never been to school."
Three words, three words, three words — and then four — and you have an entire life's desolation laid out like an inventory.
What is remarkable is that Dickens does not sentimentalise this — not yet.
He is recording, not pleading — and that restraint makes the plea all the more powerful.
The legal dimension here is worth dwelling on, because it is not incidental — it is the whole mechanism.
Jo is rejected as a witness because he cannot demonstrate sufficient understanding of the oath — he does not know what will be done to him, in any formal religious sense, if he lies.
And yet Dickens shows us, with some care, that Jo does know something about truth and consequence.
He knows, as the passage puts it, that:
"it'll be something wery bad to punish him, and serve him right — and so he'll tell the truth."
The irony is exquisite and savage: the boy who cannot be sworn in to give evidence is the one character in the room whose moral instinct about truth-telling is entirely sound.
The law's exclusion of Jo is not an accident or a hard case — it is a structural feature.
James is right that it's structural, and I want to push on exactly what that structure is doing.
The law doesn't exclude Jo by accident, or even by indifference — it excludes him because he has nothing the system recognises as social standing.
No name beyond a single syllable. No family. No school. No property. No church membership to ground an oath.
He is, in the most literal Victorian legal sense, nobody.
And then we get to what Jo does know — and it concerns the dead man, Nemo.
Dickens gives us the scene of their first meeting — that cold winter night — and the single line Nemo speaks is everything.
"Neither have I. Not one!"
Two men at the absolute bottom of the social order, recognising each other across the darkness — that is the solidarity the system cannot account for, and cannot permit.
I would gently resist the word solidarity, if I may — not because the feeling isn't real, but because I think it's something more particular than a class alliance.
What Nemo offers Jo is not solidarity in any political sense — it is simply kindness.
The passage is careful about this: when Nemo had money, he gave some; when he had none, he said so.
He asked whether the boy slept sound, whether he ever wished to die — questions of pastoral care, not political consciousness.
And the narrator endorses it in exactly those terms — as something approaching grace.
"There is something like a distant ray of light in thy muttered reason for this: 'He wos wery good to me, he wos!'"
A distant ray of light — not a beacon, not a programme — just enough to see by, in a very dark room.
I take Edmund's point — and I don't want to turn Nemo into a Chartist pamphlet.
But I think the novel is doing something very deliberate with the word 'graceless' — which is what it calls Jo just before that ray of light appears.
'That graceless creature' — who has been given no church, no education, no name worth spelling — is the one the narrator then turns to with something approaching tenderness.
The irony is theological as much as social: the institutions that are supposed to dispense grace have produced gracelessness.
And then what actually functions as grace — a bowl of soup, the price of a night's lodging — comes from another man with nothing.
This is where the inquest scene earns its comedy too, and I think we shouldn't let it pass.
Mrs. Piper's testimony is placed immediately before Jo's, and the contrast is devastating.
She is accepted as a credible witness — she has a husband, a child, a home, a name — and what she produces is this:
"the plaintive — so Mrs. Piper insists on calling the deceased — was reported to have sold himself."
Rumour, malapropism, a dream about a pickaxe — this is what the court admits as evidence about the dead man's character.
The legal system credits the garrulous property-owner and discredits the silent, truthful pauper.
That is not a satirical exaggeration — that is approximately how it worked.
Mrs. Piper is also — and this is easily overlooked — genuinely funny.
The sentences pile on clause after clause, each one undercutting the last — the parenthetical mention of little Alexander James Piper, aged eighteen months, is pure Dickensian abundance.
But the comedy is doing moral work — it is showing us the texture of testimony that the court finds entirely acceptable.
Johnson once observed that the law is not made for the convenience of the public, but for the convenience of the lawyers — Dickens arrives at a very similar verdict here, by different means.
And it's not limited to the inquest — the same machinery appears again, much later in the novel, when the legal system defends itself against reform.
There is a passage in Chapter Thirty-Nine — Mr. Kenge defending the existence of practitioners like Vholes against a client who has been ruined by them — that takes the breath away.
The argument isn't that the law is just — the argument is that the law employs people.
Kenge says, and I want to quote this exactly because the parody is so precise:
"Sir, that class of practitioners would be swept from the face of the earth."
And the parliamentary inquiry — which Dickens imagines in devastating detail — ends when a single answer proves fatal to the inquiry for ten years.
'Mr. Vholes is considered, in the profession, a MOST respectable man.' — Respectability as the ultimate kill switch on reform.
The parliamentary committee passage is one of the most accurate satirical renditions of a Select Committee inquiry I have ever read — and I have read a great many actual ones.
The numbered questions, the evasive answers, the final unanswerable appeal to professional reputation — it is precisely how reform is smothered.
The connection to Jo is direct: the boy is excluded from testimony because he lacks social credentials; the law protects itself from scrutiny by invoking social credentials.
The same mechanism operates in both directions.
I want to come back, if I may, to something that sits somewhat apart from the legal machinery — though it is not unrelated to it.
There is a passage assigned to Daniel's area that I find extraordinarily moving — Jenny speaking about her dead child.
She says:
"It's my dead child that makes me love this child so dear, and it's my dead child that makes her love it so dear too...
we mean the same thing, if we knew how to say it, us two mothers does in our poor hearts!"
'If we knew how to say it' — there is Dickens's understanding of his own task.
The novelist gives voice to those who don't have the language to speak their own grief — that is, if you'll forgive the expression, a form of grace.
Edmund has found the passage I was building toward, and he's right that it's extraordinary.
What I'd add is that Jenny and Liz are not simply figures of sentiment — they are figures of knowledge.
They understand their situation — the precariousness of the child, the bond between them — with a clarity that the respectable characters entirely lack.
'We mean the same thing, if we knew how to say it' — the knowledge is there; only the socially recognised form of speech is absent.
Which is exactly Jo's position at the inquest: the truth is there; only the legal credential to speak it is withheld.
That connection — between Jenny's inarticulate knowledge and Jo's excluded testimony — feels like the spine of everything we've been discussing today.
The novel keeps returning to those who know and feel with perfect accuracy, but who are denied the forms in which that knowledge can be heard.
Edmund Leigh, James Blackstone, Daniel Rosen — thank you.
In our next segment, we'll turn from the witnesses to the institution itself — Chancery — and ask what it means that the novel's great fog is not a metaphor but a courtroom.
Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked.
We've been tracing the architecture of a novel that builds its world out of fog, delay, and the slow ruin of almost everything it loves.
Today we turn to one of the novel's most painful trajectories — the descent of Richard Carstone.
Richard begins the novel as one of its most promising young figures — warm, charming, full of appetite for life.
And we watch Jarndyce and Jarndyce eat him alive.
With us to unpick how and why that happens are three voices whose arguments, I suspect, will not always agree.
Sir Edmund Leigh brings the moral imagination of a great Oxford critic — for him, Richard's story is above all a story about character.
Professor James Blackstone locates Richard inside the actual legal machinery that destroyed real lives — he knows what Chancery cost in flesh and money.
And Dr. Daniel Rosen will argue, I imagine, that Richard's tragedy is structural — that the novel shows us a system producing ruin, not merely a young man who failed to resist it.
Edmund, let's begin with you — and with Jarndyce himself, because it's through Jarndyce's counsel that we first understand what Richard is being asked to become.
Thank you.
The passages in Chapter Thirteen are, for me, among the most carefully poised in the entire novel.
Jarndyce is not preaching — he is reasoning, with affection.
And what he says to Richard carries the full weight of what the novel ultimately asks of every character.
He puts it with extraordinary directness.
"Trust in nothing but in Providence and your own efforts. Never separate the two, like the heathen waggoner."
That phrase — the heathen waggoner — is doing rather a lot of work.
Jarndyce is invoking the old story of the man who prays for his cart to be moved from the mire, but does not put his shoulder to the wheel.
Richard will of course do precisely that — he will wait upon Fortune rather than earn his place.
Jarndyce sees it coming, and says so, with remarkable gentleness.
I want to hold that gentleness up to the light for a moment, because it matters historically.
Jarndyce is a Chancery ward himself — he has lived inside this system and come out, barely, on the other side.
He knows, with the precision of a survivor, exactly what the suit does to a young mind that allows it purchase.
And so this counsel is not abstract morality — it is hard-won intelligence about an institution that Dickens documented with forensic care.
Chancery proceedings in the 1840s and 50s could run for decades, generating costs that regularly devoured entire estates.
Jarndyce and Jarndyce is exaggerated, yes — but not by very much.
So when Jarndyce tells Richard, almost tenderly, that this chain of flowers he has taken up is very easily broken, or might become a chain of lead — that image is not decorative.
"this chain of flowers you have taken up is very easily broken, or it might become a chain of lead."
He is describing the mechanism of Chancery itself — the slow transformation of hope into bondage.
Both of those readings are right, but I think we need to press further.
Jarndyce's counsel is wise and generous — and it is also, quietly, a counsel of resignation.
What he is really telling Richard is: do not expect anything from the system. Expect only from yourself.
That is very easy advice to give when you are already comfortably settled at Bleak House.
But Richard is a ward of court — he has no settled income, no profession, no inheritance he can actually touch.
The suit is not merely a psychological temptation for Richard — it is a material condition that shapes what he can and cannot do.
The novel knows this, even when Jarndyce doesn't quite say it.
I should push back on that, and I shall — gently.
Dickens gives us other characters in equally straitened circumstances who do not yield to the suit's enchantment.
The novel is interested in what Richard chooses, not only in what is done to him.
Jarndyce is explicit about this — listen to what he says about sincerity of purpose.
"If you had the abilities of all the great men, past and present, you could do nothing well without sincerely meaning it and setting about it."
That is not a counsel of resignation — that is a statement about the nature of moral effort.
Richard's failure is, at its heart, a failure of will — not of circumstance alone.
I'd locate the two of you somewhere between disagreement and talking past each other — with respect to both.
What the novel shows us — structurally, across these chapters — is Jarndyce trying, with extraordinary care, to give Richard the tools to survive an institution that is designed to consume him.
His generosity to both Ada and Richard is, in this context, almost poignant.
He tells them, with real warmth — and I am paraphrasing now — that if they change, if they find they are more commonplace cousins than they once supposed, they should not be ashamed.
"don't be ashamed still to confide in me, for there will be nothing monstrous or uncommon in it."
He is building a safety net for them — and Richard, in the event, refuses to use it.
That refusal is both a character failure and — Daniel is right about this — a product of his position.
And what the novel shows us, just as clearly, is what the system does to those who have no Jarndyce to catch them.
Think of that extraordinary, brutal passage in Chapter Eight — Ada stooping to touch an infant's face.
Esther narrates it with a compression that is almost unbearable.
"Ada, whose gentle heart was moved by its appearance, bent down to touch its little face. As she did so, I saw what happened and drew her back. The child died."
Three sentences.
The poverty that kills that child is the other face of the fortune Jarndyce and Jarndyce has swallowed up for generations.
Richard's descent is tragic — but that child's death is the novel's reminder that tragedy is not equally distributed.
That is a powerful juxtaposition, and I accept the force of it.
And yet Dickens does something equally arresting with characters at the opposite end of the social register — characters who feel nothing at all.
Tulkinghorn stands in that same room at the novel's edge, utterly sealed.
Dickens describes him in a formulation I find endlessly fascinating.
"As easily might the tone of a delicate musical instrument be inferred from its case, as the tone of Mr. Tulkinghorn from his case."
He has shown neither patience nor impatience, nor attention nor abstraction — only his shell.
Tulkinghorn is what the law produces at the top of the hierarchy — a man so perfectly enclosed in function that the person within has become invisible, perhaps even to himself.
That image of Tulkinghorn really is one of the novel's great technical achievements.
Tulkinghorn is the law's instrument — not its beneficiary, not even, in any meaningful sense, its agent.
He holds secrets for the powerful because that is what the powerful require.
And Dickens shows him, in that scene, standing aloof by the old portmanteau — physically set apart from every form of human response present in the room.
Apart from the surgeon's professional interest, apart from the old man's unction, apart from the little crazy woman's awe.
He is outside all of it — and that is precisely his value to the Dedlocks.
Tulkinghorn and Richard Carstone are mirror images of each other — and I think the novel intends us to see that.
Richard is consumed by the system's promise — he gives everything to it, and it takes everything from him.
Tulkinghorn has been consumed too — but he was consumed long ago, and what remains is pure utility.
He has shown nothing but his shell — as Edmund quoted.
That is what the law's full servants look like when they are done with.
Richard at least retains enough of himself to suffer.
That is very finely put.
And it connects, I think, to one further passage that deserves our attention — the remarkable scene in Chapter Fifty-Six, when Bucket comes to Jarndyce for Esther.
It is a different kind of urgency — a detective's urgency — but it throws the same cold light on how the system treats its most vulnerable.
Bucket makes his case to Jarndyce with a precision that is almost lawyerly — and entirely human.
"If I follow her alone, she, being in ignorance of what Sir Leicester Dedlock, Baronet, has communicated to me, may be driven to desperation."
Bucket knows that a woman's survival depends not on the law's machinery, but on a single act of human recognition.
That is the novel's own deepest argument — that institutions cannot save us; only persons can.
And Bucket is himself one of the novel's most ambiguous figures in that respect.
He is an agent of the state — a professional — and yet here he speaks as one who reads human distress with something approaching compassion.
He tells Jarndyce: "if ever delay was dangerous, it's dangerous now; and if ever you couldn't afterwards forgive yourself for causing it, this is the time."
He is appealing, deliberately, to Jarndyce's moral imagination — because that is the only instrument that will work.
The law has nothing in its arsenal for a woman on the edge of despair.
Which brings us, I think, to the heart of what this novel keeps returning to — the gap between institutions and the human beings they were supposed to serve.
Richard gets consumed by one such institution; Lady Dedlock is hunted by another; and the child in Chapter Eight is simply left outside them all.
In our next segment, we'll be looking at how the novel's fog — its famous, omnipresent atmosphere — functions as more than scene-setting.
Whether it is, as Edmund would have it, a masterly literary device — or whether it is, as Daniel might argue, the smell of a system in slow decay.

segments.title: Secrets and Surveillance: The Lady's Burden

utterances.text: Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked.
We've been working our way through one of the great novels in the English language, and today we arrive at something genuinely thrilling.
Secrets. Surveillance. A woman who has everything — and one man who may know the one thing that could destroy her.
We're looking at the passages in Chapter Twelve where Dickens begins to draw the net around Lady Dedlock — and at the extraordinary figure of Mr. Tulkinghorn who holds the other end of it.
With me today are Sir Edmund Leigh, whose instinct is always to ask what these scenes tell us about individual character under moral pressure.
Professor James Blackstone, who brings the legal and institutional world that Dickens is drawing on into sharp historical focus.
And Dr. Daniel Rosen, who will, I suspect, want us to think carefully about who holds power in these rooms, and why.
Edmund, let's begin with you — because the scene where Sir Leicester reads Tulkinghorn's letter aloud is, in some ways, almost farcical, and yet the stakes couldn't be higher.
It is a masterpiece of dramatic irony, and Dickens deploys it with a kind of savage gentleness.
Sir Leicester fumbles with his eye-glass, loses his place in the letter, wanders into 'the matter of the right of way' before finding the relevant passage.
He is the engine of his wife's destruction, and he hasn't the faintest idea.
What Dickens gives us in that letter is, of course, the thunderbolt itself — and the text reads it to us via the most unwitting of couriers.
Tulkinghorn writes, with his characteristic, velvet menace:
'I have something to tell her on her return in reference to the person who copied the affidavit in the Chancery suit, which so powerfully stimulated her curiosity. I have seen him.'
Three words at the end. 'I have seen him.' The sentence is a trap door.
And Sir Leicester reads it as though it were a note about the parish rates.
And the institutional machinery behind those three words is worth pausing on.
Tulkinghorn is the Dedlocks' family solicitor — a man whose entire professional existence depends on knowing things that other people don't.
He is not employed to protect Lady Dedlock. He is employed to protect the Dedlock interest — which is a rather different thing.
Dickens describes him with extraordinary precision — and I think this is the passage that defines him more completely than anything else in the novel.
'He carries family secrets in every limb of his body and every crease of his dress.'
Every crease of his dress. The man is a walking archive.
And then Dickens goes further: 'He is his own client in that matter, and will never betray himself.'
The legal relationship is inverted. He manages his own secret as he manages theirs — professionally, impenetrably.
What James is identifying is the core of the thing, I think.
Tulkinghorn doesn't serve Lady Dedlock. He doesn't even, finally, serve Sir Leicester.
He serves the system — the system of aristocratic property and inheritance that requires secrecy to reproduce itself across generations.
And Lady Dedlock is both a beneficiary of that system and its most vulnerable point.
Look at how Dickens stages their first real confrontation — the watching, the mutual calculation.
'During the utterance of every word of this short dialogue, Lady Dedlock and Mr. Tulkinghorn, without any other alteration in their customary deportment, have looked very steadily at one another.'
Not a muscle moves in either face. The performance of aristocratic calm is itself the battleground.
And behind it — what each would give to know what the other knows. That is the real economy of this scene.
I wouldn't quarrel with that entirely, though I'd resist the word economy — it rather flattens what is, to my mind, also a moral drama.
Tulkinghorn is not merely a functionary of the class system. He is a study in a particular kind of will — cold, patient, implacable.
And Lady Dedlock's tragedy is that she encounters this will at precisely the moment when her own composure begins to crack.
Dickens renders their subsequent meetings with a phrase I find extraordinarily haunting.
'Lady Dedlock is always the same exhausted deity, surrounded by worshippers, and terribly liable to be bored to death, even while presiding at her own shrine.'
Exhausted deity. That is a characterisation of extraordinary sympathy and precision.
She is worshipped — and entirely alone.
And her aloneness has a very specific legal dimension that I think matters here.
We learn, through John Jarndyce's account to Esther, that this woman — Lady Dedlock, as we come to understand — had communicated with absolute secrecy about her connection to a child.
She used an assumed name. She refused all personal contact. She would speak only through an intermediary.
And the terms Jarndyce reports are quite remarkable in their finality.
'More than this she would never — and he was well persuaded of the steadfastness of her resolution — for any human consideration disclose.'
'For any human consideration.' That phrase is doing real work.
This is a woman who has already, years before Tulkinghorn appears on that terrace, constructed the entire architecture of her own concealment.
She didn't need Tulkinghorn to teach her surveillance. She was already practising it on herself.
That is exactly right, and it changes the moral geometry of the whole situation.
Lady Dedlock isn't a passive victim waiting to be exposed. She is an active agent of her own suppression.
Which is itself a product of the system — the system demanded that she suppress it or be destroyed, and she chose survival.
And then Dickens delivers what I think is the novel's most devastating sentence about what that survival costs.

'Whether each evermore watches and suspects the other, evermore mistrustful of some great reservation; whether each is evermore prepared at all points for the other, and never to be taken unawares; what each would give to know how much the other knows — all this is hidden, for the time, in their own hearts.'
Hidden in their own hearts. Not resolved. Not known even to themselves with certainty.
The novel refuses to let us inside either mind fully. That refusal is itself a structural argument about the cost of secrecy.
When a society makes certain truths unspeakable, even the people carrying those truths lose access to themselves.
I find that reading genuinely compelling — and I say so without abandoning my own sense that Dickens was also writing something older than any social critique.
The structure of this story — the secret, the witness, the slow tightening — is as old as tragedy.
Lady Dedlock is not merely a woman victimised by Victorian property law. She is a figure who made a choice — and is now living within it.
And what Dickens has the rare courage to show is that the performance of composure — 'her usual fatigued manner and insolent grace' — has become indistinguishable from the woman herself.
She is not pretending to be Lady Dedlock. She has become her. That is the real horror.
The mask that becomes the face — and the lawyer who may be the only one who remembers there was ever a face beneath it.
That feels like a very fine place to pause.
Edmund Leigh, James Blackstone, Daniel Rosen — thank you.
We'll be back shortly to follow the fog further into the Court of Chancery — and the lives it quietly ruins.

segments.title: The System Exposed: Class and Complicity

utterances.text: Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked.
Today we're looking at how Dickens exposes the machinery of class — the invisible wires by which the powerful are, in fact, managed.
And how, at the other end of that system, the most invisible people leave almost no trace at all.
Joining me are Sir Edmund Leigh, retired Oxford don and moral-imaginative reader of fiction in the grand tradition.
Professor James Blackstone, legal and social historian, who knows precisely what these institutions cost in human terms.
And Dr. Daniel Rosen, cultural historian, who reads every drawing room as a site of class power.
James, I'd like to start with you — because Dickens opens this analysis in a most unexpected place: the jeweller's counter.
Yes — and what Dickens is doing with Lady Dedlock's world is really quite subversive, in a way that can slip past a casual reader.
Lady Dedlock believes herself to be — and the novel's phrasing is exact here — an inscrutable Being, quite out of the reach of ordinary mortals.
But every tradesperson, every servant, every dim little star in her orbit has taken an accurate measure of her moral nature.
Dickens gives us the jewellers Blaze and Sparkle, the mercers Sheen and Gloss, the librarian Mr. Sladdery — each of them perfectly candid about the technique.
And then he lands this extraordinary image — let me read it:
"who, in hooking one, hook all and bear them off as Lemuel Gulliver bore away the stately fleet of the majestic Lilliput."
That simile tells you everything: the aristocracy is the fleet — magnificent, stately, entirely at the mercy of the tiny figure who holds the string.
In historical terms, this is Dickens identifying the consumer culture of the 1850s as the engine that actually drives aristocratic behaviour — not the other way round.
James is right that the satire is wonderfully precise — but I'd resist the word subversive.
Dickens isn't dismantling the class system here — he's doing something older and, I think, richer: he is exposing vanity.
The great moralists — from Johnson to Burke — were always fascinated by the self-deception of the powerful.
Lady Dedlock sees herself in her glass, and she looks inscrutable there — and that is the joke, and it is a moral joke.
The Gulliver image is comic genius, but the target is her credulity about herself — not the mercantile system that surrounds her.
I don't think we need to choose between those readings — in fact, the novel insists we don't.
The vanity Edmund describes is itself a product of the class position — it is the ideology that the class requires in order to function.
Blaze and Sparkle don't just flatter Lady Dedlock — they study her weaknesses systematically and exploit them for profit.
That is a description of a market — and a market that depends entirely on the aristocracy's refusal to know itself.
Dickens names Mr. Sladdery an honest man precisely because Sladdery is honest about this — he says without vanity: I can turn them round my finger.
The comedy and the critique are inseparable.
And yet Dickens shows us, almost in the same breath, what exists at the absolute opposite end of this world of fashion and flattery.
James — you wanted to bring us to Chapter Eleven, and to a figure who couldn't be more different from Lady Dedlock.
Nemo — the man whose very name means no one.
He dies in a garret, and Dickens renders that death with almost unbearable economy.
Here is the whole of it:
"the lonely figure on the bed, whose path in life has lain through five and forty years, lies there with no more track behind him that any one can trace than a deserted infant."
Forty-five years of life — and no traceable record.
In historical terms, that was entirely possible for a man of his position — no parish registration, no employer's record, no fixed address of any permanence.
The state simply did not see him — and neither, until this moment, does anyone else.
The image of the deserted infant is the key — it is not merely pathetic, it is exact.
An infant has no history because it has not yet lived — Nemo has no history because his life was lived in conditions that left no mark on the record.
That is a very different kind of invisibility from Lady Dedlock's carefully performed inscrutability.
She performs the mystery — his is simply the consequence of poverty and obscurity.
And the novel immediately supplies the one person who does see Nemo — who did see him.
Jo — the crossing-sweeper — a child even more marginal than the dead man.
And Dickens gives Jo a grief that is almost unbearable in its simplicity — listen to the phrasing:
"He wos wery good to me, he wos!"
Dickens renders Jo's dialect exactly — not to condescend, but to insist on the full reality of this child's inner life.
The only eulogy Nemo receives is from the boy the rest of society refuses to see.
That is the novel's moral architecture laid bare — solidarity exists only among those whom the system has discarded.

And if we move forward in the novel — to Chapter Sixty-Two — we find someone at the opposite extreme of comfort who has nevertheless made exactly the same moral judgment about one of its central institutions.
John Jarndyce — Esther's guardian, a man of real decency — is handed a will that could affect the entire Chancery suit.
And he will not even read it himself — and his explanation is this:
"The plain truth is, I have forsworn and abjured the whole business these many years, and my soul is sick of it."
My soul is sick of it — that is not the language of legal objection; it is the language of moral revulsion.
For a legal historian, this line is extraordinarily pointed — here is a man of property voluntarily recusing himself from the court that manages his own inheritance.
That line is among the finest in the novel, I think — and it works precisely because Jarndyce is not a radical.
He is a conservative man of feeling — and the fact that such a man's soul is sick of it tells us something that no polemicist could convey.
The indictment is all the more powerful for being uttered quietly, to his ward and a policeman, with no audience.
Quite right — and what I find remarkable is how that line connects to the novel's larger structure.
Jarndyce has refused the suit because he understands — has understood for years — that participation in Chancery is itself a form of moral contamination.
The system doesn't just waste money and time — it corrupts the people who remain inside it.
And yet — and this is the tragedy — even Jarndyce's withdrawal cannot protect the people he loves from the suit's eventual destruction.
There is no honourable private exit from a systemically corrupt institution — that is the novel's bleakest argument.
I want to bring in one more passage — because this segment has moved between the comic and the tragic, and I think the novel does something similarly unsettling with its private histories.
Jarndyce tells Esther the story of Lady Dedlock's sister — who made a sacrifice that no institution required of her, but that her own code of honour made absolute.
Jarndyce's account is precise and devastating — he says of her:

"she wrote him that from the date of that letter she died to him — as in literal truth she did — and that the resolution was exacted from her by her knowledge of his proud temper and his strained sense of honour, which were both her nature too."
And then: 'she made the sacrifice, she said, and would live in it and die in it' — and she did both.
The internalisation of an honour code so rigid that it becomes indistinguishable from a sentence — that is what the class system does to its most conscientious members as much as to its poorest ones.
That is finely observed — though I would want to insist on something the passage makes very clear: this is her choice.
Dickens says the act was hers, the motives kept in her inflexible heart — those are not the words of a novelist blaming institutions.
They are the words of a novelist who understood that human beings are capable of enormous self-destruction in the name of a principle — and that this is simultaneously noble and tragic.
And I'd say the two readings are not in conflict — because the honour code she internalises is not free-floating.
It is a code that belongs to a specific class, a specific moment — Boythorn's proud temper, his strained sense of honour.
She destroys herself not for some universal moral law, but for the particular honour culture of people like them — which were both her nature too, as Jarndyce says.
That is how class gets inside the self — not as external compulsion, but as the thing you call your own deepest nature.
From the stately fleet of Lilliput to a coffin beside an old portmanteau — Dickens holds the whole social world in a single novel.
After the break, we'll turn to the question of how Dickens renders justice — or its absence — and what the novel's ending actually argues.

segments.title: Dickens's Narrative Mirror: Technique and Truth

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, the programme that takes Dickens's great novel apart — passage by passage — to see how it works and what it means.

Today we're looking at something that sits at the very heart of the novel's genius: the way Dickens uses narrative technique — voice, irony, structural echo — to tell truths that direct statement could never quite reach.
Joining me, as always, are three remarkable readers of this novel.
Sir Edmund Leigh brings the perspective of a scholar who believes the novel's moral imagination is its truest achievement — that character under pressure is the real subject of great fiction.
Professor James Blackstone reminds us that these pages are also a historical record — that the institutions Dickens satirises were real, and their damage was measurable.
And Dr. Daniel Rosen reads the novel as an anatomy of class power — tracking precisely how the system reproduces itself through law, charity, and habit.
Edmund, I'd like to begin with you — and with one of the most ferocious passages in the whole of Bleak House: the brickmaker's speech.
What is Dickens doing here technically — and what makes it so devastating?
What strikes me first is the audacity of the device.
Dickens gives the brickmaker the initiative entirely — the man pre-empts Mrs. Pardiggle's charitable interrogation before it can begin.
He knows the script of the charity visit by heart — every question she would ask — and he answers them himself, in sequence, with savage precision.
Listen to how that accumulation of self-accusation becomes, paradoxically, the most powerful indictment of the accuser.
"Is my daughter a-washin? Yes, she IS a-washin. Look at the water. Smell it! That's wot we drinks. How do you like it, and what do you think of gin instead!"
The rhetorical form — question, bald answer, physical evidence — is borrowed directly from the charitable visitor's own method.
He has internalised the form and turned it against her — which is a kind of genius, on Dickens's part, of the most uncomfortable sort.
Edmund is right about the rhetorical inversion, and I'd add a historical layer.
The brickmaker's monologue is also a precise documentary account of what poverty in a brickmaking settlement actually looked like in mid-Victorian England.
The water — drinking from the same source used for washing and likely shared with animals — was a genuine cause of the cholera outbreaks that killed thousands.
And five dead infants — that is not melodrama; that is the infant mortality rate in overcrowded brick-working communities.
What makes Dickens extraordinary is that he embeds this social fact in dialect speech, so it arrives as the character's own testimony rather than a reformer's report.
The grammar is broken; the evidence is not.
And yet Dickens also makes the brickmaker complicit in his own degradation — the drinking, the violence against his wife.
That is not a flaw in the politics; that is the politics.
The system doesn't simply impoverish people; it deforms them — and then points to the deformation as justification for withholding improvement.
When he says the beadle is too genteel to receive him in church, he is articulating something that Mrs. Pardiggle will never understand:
that the very institutions meant to redeem him have already categorised him as unredeemable.
That is the mechanism Dickens is exposing — and he requires no editorialising to expose it.
I won't dispute the mechanism — but I do think Daniel risks flattening the character into a case study.
Dickens gives us a man with grievance, yes — but also with volition, with a very particular furious pride.
He refuses the little book not because he cannot read — others in the room cannot either — but because it is a book fit for a baby.
That distinction matters enormously to him, and Dickens honours it.
The chapter holds something else too — a passage that Edmund, I suspect, has been thinking about since we began.
Esther's reflection on the handkerchief — a passage that seems to operate on an entirely different register from the brickmaker's rage.
Yes — and this is where I think Dickens the narrative architect reveals himself most clearly.
The brickmaker's chapter moves us from fierce social polemic to — almost without our noticing — this extraordinary moment of tenderness and prophetic shadow.
Esther covers a dead infant with her own handkerchief — a gesture of simple human kindness.
But Dickens, writing retrospectively through Esther's voice, allows her to look back at that moment with a knowledge she didn't yet have.

"How little I thought, when I raised my handkerchief to look upon the tiny sleeper underneath — how little I thought in whose unquiet bosom that handkerchief would come to lie after covering the motionless and peaceful breast!"
That phrase — "unquiet bosom" against "motionless and peaceful breast" — is the whole tragedy of Lady Dedlock compressed into eight words.
Dickens is planting a seed in a chapter about brickmakers and philanthropy that will flower, devastatingly, more than forty chapters later.
There's something else worth noting about that passage structurally.
The halo that Esther perceives around Ada's drooping head — Ada's pity bending her toward the dead infant of the poor — that is not sentiment.
It is Dickens encoding a structural irony: the women of the upper classes can perform compassion at the moment of death, but cannot prevent the conditions that caused it.
The handkerchief becomes an object that migrates across class lines — and what it carries with it is not comfort, but tragedy.
And that migration — the handkerchief appearing later on Lady Dedlock — tells us something precise about how the novel is structured as a system of connections.
Nothing in this novel is simply decorative.
Objects, phrases, names — they all carry legal and social weight, and they travel.
One might say that Dickens understands what equity lawyers understand — that a chain of title, once established, cannot simply be wished away.
Let's turn to another kind of technique — one that operates not through tenderness but through ice.
Vholes — the solicitor who manages Richard Carstone's affairs — and a passage that Edmund finds, I think, instructive in a particular way.
Vholes is one of Dickens's most brilliantly sustained satirical creations — and what makes him so is the precision of the technique.
He is never simply villainous — he is always correctly, procedurally, professionally right.
He tells Esther, with complete candour, that Richard's affairs are in a very bad way and the marriage ill-advised.
"I regard it in the light of a professional duty to be so, though it can be charged to no one."
There is the whole horror of Vholes in one sentence.
He performs a duty that cannot be billed — because its true function is not information but the performance of propriety.
Meanwhile, of course, his clock keeps running and his diary keeps filling.
The diary is the key detail, for me.
Vholes notes that he happened afterwards to note his words in his diary — and that the diary is producible at any time.
This is a man who documents his own virtue in real time, as a legal instrument.
The law doesn't just permit this — the law requires this kind of documentation.
Dickens understands that a system which rewards the appearance of procedure over the substance of justice will produce Vholeses by the score.
Historically, Vholes is almost entirely accurate — right down to the diary.
Solicitors in Chancery practice were expected to keep contemporaneous notes of advice given — it was part of protecting themselves from later accusations of negligence.
What Dickens sees — and this is the satirical precision Edmund is pointing at — is that the protection of the professional is indistinguishable from the performance of the professional.
And the client — Richard Carstone — cannot tell the difference. Which is, of course, fatal.
Before we close this segment, Edmund — Sir Leicester Dedlock.
Because Dickens does something technically very surprising with him — and it connects, I think, to everything we've been saying about how the narrator positions moral judgment.
Sir Leicester is, for much of the novel, a magnificent object of satire — stiff, antiquated, proud to the point of absurdity.
And then the narrator — the omniscient narrator, not Esther — performs one of the most remarkable reversals in all of Victorian fiction.
At the moment of his wife's disgrace, the narrator lifts Sir Leicester entirely clear of class and looks at him as a human being.
"His noble earnestness, his fidelity, his gallant shielding of her, his generous conquest of his own wrong and his own pride for her sake, are simply honourable, manly, and true."
And then the narrator draws the conclusion that demolishes class distinction altogether.
"In such a light both aspire alike, both rise alike, both children of the dust shine equally."
That is not irony. That is not satire. It is Dickens reaching for something closer to theodicy.
It is one of the passages I find most difficult to argue with — and I say that as someone who spends considerable time arguing with Dickens.
The redemption of Sir Leicester is earned within the logic of the novel — his pride was always also a form of loyalty.
But I notice that "children of the dust" does not say that the dust is equally distributed.
It says that in the light of moral quality — of earnestness, fidelity, genuine feeling — the aristocrat and the mechanic are equivalent.
That is not the same as saying the structures of inequality should be dismantled.
Dickens was more radical than this passage — and less radical than this passage — depending on which chapter you are in.
That is a fair tension to hold, I think.
Dickens is writing inside a class system and imagining a moral equality that the class system does not provide and does not threaten to provide.
Sir Leicester gets to be noble in defeat; the brickmaker's children are simply dead.
The novel holds both realities simultaneously — and that is precisely the kind of structural honesty that no pamphlet could achieve.
The novel holds both realities simultaneously — and that, perhaps, is the most precise description of what narrative technique actually does in Dickens's hands.
Thank you, Edmund, James, Daniel — we'll continue after a short break.
We've spent this episode tracing the long shadow that Jarndyce and Jarndyce casts over the young people caught within it.
And I want to close by returning to Richard Carstone — because his story feels, in some ways, like the novel's central warning.
Edmund, let's begin with you — Richard and Ada, and what Esther sees when she watches them leave.
The passage is one of the most quietly devastating in the entire novel, and Dickens achieves it with almost no apparent effort.
Esther watches Richard and Ada pass through a sunlit room — heads bent together, full of youth and tenderness.
And then Dickens gives us this:

"So young, so beautiful, so full of hope and promise, they went on lightly through the sunlight as their own happy thoughts might then be traversing the years to come and making them all years of brightness."
"So they passed away into the shadow and were gone."
That word 'passed away' does immense work — it is not merely departure, it is an intimation of mortality.
This is Dickens at his most morally serious — showing us that hope, if it is founded on the wrong things, already contains its own extinction.
Edmund is right that it's devastating, but I'd push on where the destruction originates.
The clouding of the sun is not fate acting on character — it is an institution acting on people.
Richard's deterioration is not a flaw waiting inside him to emerge — it is produced by the court's endless deferral.
And we already have an early signal of it in how Mrs. Badger describes him — not as wicked, but as structurally misaligned with real work.
She says Richard lacks, in her words,
"that positive interest in it which makes it his vocation."
Now, Dickens frames that as personal deficiency — but what has Richard been raised on?
The promise of an inheritance that will one day arrive and make striving unnecessary.
Mrs. Badger's comparison to Woodcourt is pointed, and historically it carries real weight.
She draws the contrast directly — men who take medicine from genuine passion will endure.
She says of Woodcourt and those like him:

"Young men like Mr. Allan Woodcourt who take it from a strong interest in all that it can do will find some reward in it through a great deal of work for a very little money and through years of considerable endurance and disappointment."
That is the actual texture of professional life in the mid-nineteenth century — very little money, considerable disappointment.
Richard has never been taught to want that — no one in his position was.
Chancery's great cruelty is precisely this: it keeps its wards just comfortable enough that necessity never sharpens them.
Blackstone makes a point I find genuinely compelling — and I say that as someone resistant to institutional explanations for moral failure.
And yet — Esther's earlier conversation with them shows something else still present in Richard at this stage.
There is real goodness in him — real willingness, however undisciplined.
Esther records that they sat together considering how love could come to happiness only — and I want to read this carefully —
"if it were real and lasting and inspired them with a steady resolution to do their duty to each other, with constancy, fortitude, and perseverance, each always for the other's sake."
Those are not sentimental virtues — constancy, fortitude, perseverance.
They are the virtues that Richard, fatally, will prove unable to sustain.
Edmund frames that as character — but I'd say Esther's counsel is itself a kind of innocence.
She believes constancy and fortitude are sufficient — that love and duty, held firmly enough, can overcome a corrupting institution.
The novel will prove her wrong on Richard's behalf — not because he lacks good impulses, but because the system is designed to convert hope into dependency.
And that image of the sun clouding over as they leave — that is not just atmosphere.
Dickens writes: "The room darkened as they went out, and the sun was clouded over."
That is a verdict — written in light.
What strikes me about all three passages is how early Dickens places his markers.
Richard's trajectory is established before he has properly begun — the languid disposition, the absent vocation, the shadowed departure.
The court does not simply destroy its victims — it does so with a terrible patience, over years.
And the novel holds both ideas simultaneously — that Richard had goodness in him, and that goodness was never going to be enough.
A verdict written in light — I think that may be where we have to leave Richard Carstone, at least for today.
There is a terrible generosity in Dickens here — he allows Richard every sympathy, and still shows us the shadow gathering.
My thanks to Sir Edmund Leigh, Professor James Blackstone, and Dr. Daniel Rosen — for a conversation that has been, I think, as rich as the novel deserves.
Bleak House Unpacked will return — there is still a great deal of darkness left to illuminate.

London. Michaelmas term lately over, and the Lord Chancellor sitting
in Lincoln’s Inn Hall. Implacable November weather. As much mud in
the streets as if the waters had but newly retired from the face of
the earth, and it would not be wonderful to meet a Megalosaurus,
forty feet long or so, waddling like an elephantine lizard up Holborn
Hill. Smoke lowering down from chimney-pots, making a soft black
drizzle, with flakes of soot in it as big as full-grown
snowflakes—gone into mourning, one might imagine, for the death of
the sun. Dogs, undistinguishable in mire. Horses, scarcely better;
splashed to their very blinkers. Foot passengers, jostling one
another’s umbrellas in a general infection of ill temper, and losing
their foot-hold at street-corners, where tens of thousands of other
foot passengers have been slipping and sliding since the day broke
(if this day ever broke), adding new deposits to the crust upon crust
of mud, sticking at those points tenaciously to the pavement, and
accumulating at compound interest.
c1:p0.summary: London in November: fog and mud pervade the entire city, creating a primordial, apocalyptic atmosphere where even extinct creatures seem plausible.
c1:p0.best_quote: As much mud in the streets as if the waters had but newly retired from the face of the earth, and it would not be wonderful to meet a Megalosaurus, forty feet long or so, waddling like an elephantine lizard up Holborn Hill.

For, on a low bed opposite the fire, a confusion of dirty patchwork,
lean-ribbed ticking, and coarse sacking, the lawyer, hesitating just
within the doorway, sees a man. He lies there, dressed in shirt and

darkness of a candle that has guttered down until the whole length of

c7:p59.text:
“She had been a lady of a handsome figure and a noble carriage. She
never complained of the change; she never spoke to any one of being
crippled or of being in pain, but day by day she tried to walk upon
the terrace, and with the help of the stone balustrade, went up and
down, up and down, up and down, in sun and shadow, with greater
difficulty every day. At last, one afternoon her husband (to whom she
had never, on any persuasion, opened her lips since that night),
standing at the great south window, saw her drop upon the pavement.
He hastened down to raise her, but she repulsed him as he bent over
her, and looking at him fixedly and coldly, said, ‘I will die here
where I have walked. And I will walk here, though I am in my grave. I
will walk here until the pride of this house is humbled. And when
calamity or when disgrace is coming to it, let the Dedlocks listen
for my step!’”
c7:p59.summary: The crippled lady, after her husband finds her on the pavement, looks at him coldly and curses the Dedlock family: she will walk the terrace forever as a warning of coming calamity and disgrace.
c7:p59.best_quote: I will die here where I have walked. And I will walk here, though I am in my grave. I will walk here until the pride of this house is humbled. And when calamity or when disgrace is coming to it, let the Dedlocks listen for my step!

That graceless creature only knows that the dead man (whom he
recognized just now by his yellow face and black hair) was sometimes
hooted and pursued about the streets. That one cold winter night when
he, the boy, was shivering in a doorway near his crossing, the man
turned to look at him, and came back, and having questioned him and
found that he had not a friend in the world, said, “Neither have I.

slept sound at night, and how he bore cold and hunger, and whether he
ever wished to die, and similar strange questions. That when the man
had no money, he would say in passing, “I am as poor as you to-day,

heartily believes) been glad to give him some.
c11:p87.summary: Jo reveals the dead man recognized him, showed him kindness, asked about his welfare, and when poor himself, shared what little he had.
c11:p87.best_quote: Neither have I. Not one! and gave him the price of a supper and a night's lodging.

Jo, is it thou? Well, well! Though a rejected witness, who “can’t
exactly say” what will be done to him in greater hands than men’s,
thou art not quite in outer darkness. There is something like a
distant ray of light in thy muttered reason for this: “He wos wery
good to me, he wos!”
c11:p100.summary: The narrator directly addresses Jo, acknowledging his legal rejection but affirming that his love for the dead man is a form of grace and light.
c11:p100.best_quote: There is something like a distant ray of light in thy muttered reason for this: 'He wos wery good to me, he wos!'

good thing, but it means nothing, and is nothing, without constancy

meaning it and setting about it. If you entertain the supposition

attention all along—“I speak to you as a gentleman of a humane
heart, and under such pressing circumstances as don’t often happen.
If ever delay was dangerous, it’s dangerous now; and if ever you
couldn’t afterwards forgive yourself for causing it, this is the
time. Eight or ten hours, worth, as I tell you, a hundred pound
apiece at least, have been lost since Lady Dedlock disappeared. I am
charged to find her. I am Inspector Bucket. Besides all the rest
that’s heavy on her, she has upon her, as she believes, suspicion of
murder. If I follow her alone, she, being in ignorance of what Sir
Leicester Dedlock, Baronet, has communicated to me, may be driven to
desperation. But if I follow her in company with a young lady,
answering to the description of a young lady that she has a
tenderness for—I ask no question, and I say no more than that—she
will give me credit for being friendly. Let me come up with her and
be able to have the hold upon her of putting that young lady for’ard,
and I’ll save her and prevail with her if she is alive. Let me come
up with her alone—a hard matter—and I’ll do my best, but I don’t
answer for what the best may be. Time flies; it’s getting on for one
o’clock. When one strikes, there’s another hour gone, and it’s worth
a thousand pound now instead of a hundred.”

c12:p67.text:
At length, one afternoon a little before sunset, when the bright
groups of figures which have for the last hour or two enlivened the
Ghost’s Walk are all dispersed and only Sir Leicester and my Lady
remain upon the terrace, Mr. Tulkinghorn appears. He comes towards
them at his usual methodical pace, which is never quickened, never
slackened. He wears his usual expressionless mask—if it be a
mask—and carries family secrets in every limb of his body and every
crease of his dress. Whether his whole soul is devoted to the great

personal secret. He keeps it, as he keeps the secrets of his clients;

Has Mr. Tulkinghorn any idea of this himself? It may be so, or it may
not, but there is this remarkable circumstance to be noted in
everything associated with my Lady Dedlock as one of a class—as one
of the leaders and representatives of her little world. She supposes
herself to be an inscrutable Being, quite out of the reach and ken of
ordinary mortals—seeing herself in her glass, where indeed she looks
so. Yet every dim little star revolving about her, from her maid to
the manager of the Italian Opera, knows her weaknesses, prejudices,
follies, haughtinesses, and caprices and lives upon as accurate a
calculation and as nice a measure of her moral nature as her
dressmaker takes of her physical proportions. Is a new dress, a new
custom, a new singer, a new dancer, a new form of jewellery, a new
dwarf or giant, a new chapel, a new anything, to be set up? There are
deferential people in a dozen callings whom my Lady Dedlock suspects
of nothing but prostration before her, who can tell you how to manage
her as if she were a baby, who do nothing but nurse her all their
lives, who, humbly affecting to follow with profound subservience,
lead her and her whole troop after them; who, in hooking one, hook
all and bear them off as Lemuel Gulliver bore away the stately fleet
of the majestic Lilliput. “If you want to address our people, sir,”
say Blaze and Sparkle, the jewellers—meaning by our people Lady
Dedlock and the rest—“you must remember that you are not dealing
with the general public; you must hit our people in their weakest
place, and their weakest place is such a place.” “To make this
article go down, gentlemen,” say Sheen and Gloss, the mercers, to
their friends the manufacturers, “you must come to us, because we
know where to have the fashionable people, and we can make it
fashionable.” “If you want to get this print upon the tables of my
high connexion, sir,” says Mr. Sladdery, the librarian, “or if you
want to get this dwarf or giant into the houses of my high connexion,
sir, or if you want to secure to this entertainment the patronage of
my high connexion, sir, you must leave it, if you please, to me, for
I have been accustomed to study the leaders of my high connexion,
sir, and I may tell you without vanity that I can turn them round my
finger”—in which Mr. Sladdery, who is an honest man, does not
exaggerate at all.

c13:p99.summary: Richard and Ada confide to Esther their mutual love, placing themselves on either side of her. Esther counsels them about the demands of enduring love and promises to speak to Mr. Jarndyce.
c13:p99.best_quote: They went on in their own wild way for a little while—I never stopped them; I enjoyed it too much myself—and then we gradually fell to considering how young they were, and how there must be a lapse of several years before this early love could come to anything, and how it could come to happiness only if it were real and lasting and inspired them with a steady resolution to do their duty to each other, with constancy, fortitude, and perseverance, each always for the other's sake.
